source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's Carrollton campus publishes 45 MW of IT capacity, third-largest in Texas and 9.5% of the 475 MW the state's operators have disclosed.

That Texas total is a floor, not a measurement. The state has 133 mapped data center facilities, and only 19 of them publish a megawatt figure at all. The disclosed subset is whoever chose to disclose, so any state-level capacity count built from it understates what is actually sitting on Texas grids. For AI planning this matters directly, because the binding question is where power and shell space already exist, and most of the state's inventory is invisible to that question.

The 45 MW is nameplate IT load, not consumption. Nothing in the record states how much of it is built out, leased, or running accelerators. The rack and GPU counts that follow from a density assumption are arithmetic on a capacity number, not an observation of deployed hardware. The certifications, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FISMA, SSAE 16 Type II and TIA-942, speak to suitability for regulated enterprise workloads, which is a different claim from AI training readiness.

What the data does not cover is as important as what it does. There is no tenant mix, no power source or interconnection detail, and no announced expansion, which the suitability score of 71 explicitly flags as missing. That score rests only on published IT capacity and operator type, so it measures disclosed size and operator category rather than any judgment about AI workloads. The 600,000 square feet of technical space and the 45 MW describe an envelope. Whether GPUs land inside it depends on decisions the spec page does not record.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
